# Research status

**Current focus:** Diagnose why the frozen 13-question CS cohort has no direct outcome labels, then test a separately frozen, more outcome-observable historical cohort without relabeling the original one. Paper 4 is being used to select reproducible falsification tests; no planner utility has been validated.

**Latest checkpoint (2026-10-15):** The separate 16-paper cohort is now fully screened and bounded-follow-up audited. It has 12 eligible questions and 4 ineligible source papers. The trajectory dimensions are direct resolution 0, premise refutation/revision 0, partial progress 5, independent strengthening 1, contradiction 0, scope narrowing/reformulation 3, continued explicit uncertainty 0; all 12 direct outcomes remain unadjudicated. This is a real observability result, not a Paper 3 score.

**Immediate experiment decision:** The Paper 3 readiness gate correctly returned **no score** because there are no directly adjudicated positive or negative resolution labels. The patch-explanation artifact pilot passed synthetic material/blinding checks, but real Defects4J execution is not currently feasible on this machine: no Defects4J CLI and no usable Java runtime. Human outcomes were not measured.

**Latest completed feasibility action:** A real bounded CAM worker completed the public-data audit. The result is a conditional no-go for the requested ablation: no currently verified public source jointly exposes project-linked logs, multiclass cause labels and paired software artifacts. The 2019 Ericsson binary product-fault recall remains separate from 2017 multiclass CAM accuracy. See [CAM feasibility](reports/cam_artifact_ablation_feasibility.json). The next task is the Badger dependency/metric gate.

**What is actually established:** 146/146 R2 object keys across the original and recovered manifests were remotely read and SHA-256/byte-count verified (122 original + 24 newly recovered). The local arXiv metadata corpus has 937,531 records; lexical screening selected 198,690 candidates; 407 distinct papers entered the stratified frame; 120 original PDFs were downloaded/extracted. For audit batches 8/15/30/34, 25/26 rows now have hash-verified full texts; the 2013 arXiv item is author-withdrawn and unavailable, and 24 new PDFs are now in R2. See [recovery audit](docs/RESEARCH_RECOVERY_AUDIT.md).

**Executed fresh-seed replication:** 5/5 paired seeds (4111–4115) completed under the same pinned source, jar, container digest, SQLite 3.40.0/NoREC and per-arm caps. Feedback-on minus feedback-off query-pair counts were **+265, +346, +407, +265, +299** (mean +316.4 / 4,000-attempt cap, 7.91 percentage points). The pinned logger prints the direct ratio; raw per-database rates and exact reconstructed numerators are retained. Exact sign test: two-sided *p*=0.0625, directional one-sided *p*=0.03125, n=5. **No bug-yield measurement; no distinct bug confirmed.** See [independent raw-log analysis](results/sqlancerpp_feedback_replication_4111_4115/independent_analysis.json) and [preregistration](research/experiment_preregistration_sqlancerpp_feedback_replication.md).

**Executed CPU-normalized follow-up:** Five additional preregistered pairs (4121–4125) completed with cgroup-v2 CPU counters. Feedback-on had higher successful-query-pair throughput in all five pairs: differences **+93.15, +43.99, +86.75, +73.08, +57.34 pairs per CPU-second** (mean +70.86; two-sided exact sign test *p*=0.0625). Run order was fixed (off then on); therefore this does not exclude order/time effects and is not a randomized, equal-CPU budget comparison. It still says nothing about distinct bug yield. Full raw counters and independent analysis: [CPU experiment](results/sqlancerpp_feedback_cpu_4121_4125/independent_analysis.json).

**New balanced-order equal-CPU test:** Five fresh pairs (4131–4135) each received 4.5 million cgroup CPU microseconds per arm; all ten stops and raw counters passed the preregistered tolerance. There were **no logged NoREC mismatch candidates and zero confirmed distinct bugs**. The secondary completed-database successful-pair differences were **+25, +51, +228, +393, −15** (mean +136.4; two-sided exact sign *p*=0.375). Partial interrupted databases were excluded. This weakens the proxy evidence and provides no bug-yield advantage. [Result report](reports/dbms_equal_cpu_result.json) and [independent raw-log reanalysis](results/sqlancerpp_feedback_equal_cpu_4131_4135/independent_analysis.json).

**Best research leads:** Findings 155–158 are literature-backed leads, not validated discoveries. 155 needs instrumented consenting code-review teams; 156 needs longitudinal verified security outcomes; 157 needs formal privacy accounting and multi-attribute data; 158 needs proof-regime and implementation audit. Broader ranking is in [the breakthrough radar](reports/CS_BREAKTHROUGH_RADAR.md).

**DP158 source and numerical check:** An independent one-dimensional simulation using the paper's *actual* small-`q` approximate budget matched the q=0.1 Figure 12 halt rates and step count closely (1 million trajectories per arm: P/Q halt 0.988712/0.987891; mean steps 113.136/113.149). This is exploratory after withdrawing an erroneous exact-KL preregistration. A prior vector-dimension sweep is retained as a hypothetical model only: it used the wrong budget formula, while Appendix G.2 does not clarify scalar output versus vector shorthand. Its original reporting-gap interpretation was therefore unsupported. [Full audit](reports/dp158_accountant_audit.json) and [independent analysis](results/dp158_filter_source_matched_q01/independent_analysis.json). No production accountant or matched-privacy baseline comparison has been tested.

**DP158 boundary check:** A theorem-backed conservative fixed-order RDP *reference* filter is implemented and unit-tested, but is not a certified production accountant. A separate million-path-per-arm sweep found max Gaussian-CDF discrepancy **0.01463 → 0.02815 → 0.04813 → 0.09218** at `q=0.1,0.19,0.3,0.5`, while halt rates remained near 99%. The three increases met the predeclared materiality rule after simultaneous Monte Carlo uncertainty; this confirms a finite-`q` limitation already anticipated by the paper, not a novel privacy failure. [Boundary analysis](results/dp158_regime_boundary/summary.json).

**Broad historical CS audit:** Among 52,362 lexically matched 2010–2022 records, 12,507 latest abstracts were revised after their publication-year end and are excluded from historical year-end features. The year×topic frame has 1,018 rows / 1,006 unique paper IDs across 220 populated cells. Three sampled questions received original-version full-text scrutiny: two broad formulations were already tested in the cutoff paper and down-ranked; one narrower NVD prospective-outcome question survives as a Level-1 lead. **Zero direct future outcomes adjudicated.** Metadata screening is not 1,006 full-text reviews. This is an exploratory dated evidence pair, not proof of general resolution or Paper 3 forecast accuracy; it was selected after finding the follow-up. **First bounded future-evidence triage:** All 13 locked questions were searched after source screening. [The exclusion ledger](reports/historical_blind_followup_triage_round1.json) records queries, dated primary near-misses and why they do not meet the frozen object/metric/security-definition test. For example, [2024 unmarked cycle packing](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.18878v2) does not solve the 2021 marked-vertex three-cycle question; a [2022 CCA-secure lattice IBEET construction](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1693.pdf) has not been shown here to retain the source scheme's flexible authorization. **All 13 remain unadjudicated, and no direct outcome or explicit-unresolved label is authenticated.** The source ledgers' “sealed” field records their earlier source-only state, not the present search state. The official 2022 IACR PDF endpoint returned 403 locally; a public archived full text was inspected with that provenance noted in the ledger.

**Deeper FD follow-up audit:** [The frozen database question](reports/historical_source_screen_round1.json) has an important pre-cutoff constraint: 2019 [DynFD](https://openproceedings.org/2019/conf/edbt/EDBT19_paper_32.pdf) already maintains exact FDs across data changes faster than repeated static discovery in its evaluation. This is prior-art narrowing plus a future near-match, **not a direct historical resolution label**; the question remains unadjudicated.

./docs/fulltext_audit_batch50.md:17:Theorem 1.1 gives an `(ε,δ)`-differentially private online algorithm for `k`-way marginals over records in `{0,1}^d`. It answers adaptively chosen queries with additive error at most `0.01` on every query with probability at least `0.99`, provided the database size scales as `n ≥ C d^0.51 log(|Q|) log(1/δ)/ε`; per-query runtime is polynomial in `n` and subexponential in `d`, with the stated exponent depending on `k`. An offline corollary releases all `k`-way marginals under its own database-size condition. The result is a worst-case theoretical guarantee, not a measured deployment: runtime can still be exponential-like in dimension, and privacy, accuracy, query count, and database size trade against each other. The paper explicitly notes that private multiplicative weights had shown practical performance on some databases, while independent-noise methods could fail on those databases; its improvement targets the runtime/database-size regime, not universal practical superiority. Its polynomial lower bound constrains the paper's low-weight polynomial representation approach, not every possible differentially private mechanism.
./docs/fulltext_audit_batch60.md:7:The arXiv copy is a 2011 deposit of Moshe Tennenholtz’s JAIR 17 (2002), pp. 363–378 article. The paper defines safety-level strategies and asks when their worst-case payoff compares favorably with a Nash-equilibrium payoff. Its equal-payoff results are conditional: in generic non-reducible 2×2 games, equality is shown when the safety-level strategy is strictly mixed; the paper explicitly warns that it need not hold for a pure safety-level strategy. In the extended decentralized load-balancing model, it proves a 9/8-competitive safety strategy in the many-player limit; other ratios depend on the network structure and assumptions. These are mathematical guarantees in specified games, not empirical evidence that deployed agents achieve the same ratios under model error, repeated interaction, or communication failures.
./docs/fulltext_audit_batch60.md:21:2. **Opponent-prediction guarantees are conditional and motivate calibration tests.** I-POMDP Lite’s theorem bounds policy loss in terms of opponent-strategy prediction error, while the experiments use modeled/synthetic opponents, including a scripted traffic agent over 800 episodes. The guarantee does not establish that the prediction error is small for real human drivers. A falsifiable follow-up should compare predicted-opponent policy, robust/worst-case planning, and simple baselines against held-out human and synthetic behavior while measuring calibration error, collision/near-miss rates, delay, and reward. The practical lead weakens if prediction error is poorly calibrated or improvements vanish against shifted opponent populations; it strengthens if the bound and empirical loss track one another on held-out settings.

./docs/fulltext_audit_batch58.md:19:Although this record entered arXiv in November 2013 and therefore falls in the frozen arXiv-submission stratum, its PDF is a Brandeis PhD dissertation dated August 2009. This is a discovered chronology mismatch: do not interpret it as a 2013-origin research result. The dissertation proves 0CFA decision PTIME-complete and, for the specified higher-order functional-language formulation, kCFA EXPTIME-complete for every fixed `k > 0`; it also characterizes exact kCFA as PTIME-complete. The preface explicitly says to expect proofs and theorems, not benchmarks or prototype implementations. These are formal worst-case decision-complexity results, not a claim that every practical workload necessarily exhibits exponential runtime.
./docs/fulltext_audit_batch58.md:21:The targeted PLDI 2010 follow-up “Resolving and Exploiting the k-CFA Paradox” is strong scope-correcting evidence: it explains why an identically named/formally related k-CFA is polynomial-time for object-oriented programs yet exponential-time for functional programs, due to object/closure representation, and derives a polynomial-time `m`-CFA hierarchy for functional programs. The paper also reports experiments in which m-CFA appears as precise as k-CFA at lower cost on its evaluated cases. Thus the theorem is model- and representation-specific, and there is prior empirical work on alternatives. A remaining, testable opportunity is a modern, matched replication across functional and OO encodings, separating worst-case complexity stressors from representative programs and measuring precision, time, and memory under clearly specified closure abstractions.
./docs/fulltext_audit_batch58.md:29:3. **kCFA complexity claims must be reported with language and representation.** The sampled 2009 dissertation proves a worst-case EXPTIME-completeness result for kCFA (`k > 0`) in its functional higher-order formulation, while the PLDI 2010 follow-up explains a polynomial OO case and proposes polynomial m-CFA for functional programs, with lower-cost/competitive-precision results on its own experiments. A reproducible modern comparison should pin each analysis definition, language encoding, closure representation, benchmark set, precision metric, and compute budget, then include both worst-case-generated and real-program inputs. This may confirm or revise practical tradeoffs; it cannot overturn a valid formal worst-case theorem merely by finding easy instances. The arXiv submission date is not the dissertation’s research date.

./docs/fulltext_audit_batch52.md:17:The authors resolve four previously open variants of energy/flow-time scheduling. The flow-plus-energy cases with unit weights/arbitrary sizes and arbitrary weights/unit sizes are NP-hard; corresponding energy-budget cases are also NP-hard, even with a prescribed priority order. Conversely, all considered variants with a prescribed completion-time order are solvable in polynomial time through an LP formulation. This is a structural distinction: a priority order is not equivalent to knowing the completion order. The paper also corrects a prior claimed generalization: a two-speed algorithm was asserted to extend straightforwardly to `k` speeds, but the authors give counterexamples to two natural generalizations and use a different LP approach. Its future direction is approximation of the NP-hard variants, with online `(2+ε)` competitiveness as a baseline for one flow-plus-energy case. ./docs/fulltext_audit_batch23.md:13:## 2. On the Limitations of Analysing Worst-Case Dynamic Energy of Processing (2016 arXiv; 2018 journal version)
./docs/fulltext_audit_batch23.md:17:This is a theory paper about the worst-case dynamic energy caused by operand-dependent switching in processor datapaths, not a benchmark of average energy-saving techniques. It proves exact worst-case switching is NP-hard and rules out useful constant- or polynomial-factor approximation with guaranteed safety under the formal model. Thus a safe upper bound may have to be coarse/over-pessimistic; an average instruction-energy model based on random operands is not automatically a safe worst-case bound. The paper's Xcore case study shows operand-dependent switching can be material on a deeply embedded processor.
./docs/fulltext_audit_batch23.md:19:**Counterweight and scope:** the result concerns one component of dynamic processor energy, particularly relevant when processor datapath switching is a substantial fraction of system energy. The authors note that in systems with caches, memory hierarchies, displays, peripherals, and multiple supplies, this contribution can be a smaller share of total energy. The theorem is not a claim that average workload energy cannot be measured or optimized; worst-case safety and typical/mean energy are different targets. The paper itself points toward statistical characterization as a separate route, without treating it as a safe worst-case guarantee.
./docs/fulltext_audit_batch23.md:39:In this four-paper slice, “energy” denotes at least four distinct constructs: modeled operational estimate from system counters; safe worst-case dynamic-energy bound; assumed component power multiplied by runtime; and a reported total Wh value without enough acquisition detail to reproduce it. Then have independent groups reproduce/rerank a subset using the published accounting contract. The hypothesis that explicit accounting improves reproducibility and prevents invalid rankings is weakened if these fields do not predict replication success or if rankings remain stable under reasonable boundary/meter changes. apply plugin: 'java'

def version = '0.1'

--- Badger build ---
<?xml version="1.0" ?>

<!--
  build.xml - generic JPF extension build script
              using Ant (http://jakarta.apache.org/ant)
  public targets:

    compile           compile JPF and its specific (modeled) environment libraries
    test              run all JPF tests
    jar               build JPF jar files
    dist              build binary distribution
    clean             remove the files that have been generated by the build process
-->

<project name="badger" default="build" basedir=".">

  <!-- ========================== COMMON SECTION ========================== -->

  <!--
    local props have to come first, because Ant properties are immutable
    NOTE: this file is local - it is never in the repository!
  -->
  <property file="local.properties"/>
  <property environment="env"/>

  <!-- this is where we get the 'jpf-core' location from -->
  <property file="${user.home}/.jpf/site.properties"/>

  <!-- get the jpf-core path properties -->
  <property file="${jpf-core}/jpf.properties"/>

  <!-- add dependencies on other jpf projects, e.g. on jpf-symbc -->
  <property file="${jpf-symbc}/jpf.properties"/>

  <!-- compiler settings -->
  <property name="src_level"     value="8"/>
  <property name="debug"         value="on"/>
  <property name="deprecation"   value="on"/>


  <!-- generic classpath settings -->
  <path id="lib.path">

    <!-- add in what we need from the core -->
    <pathelement path="${jpf-core.native_classpath}"/>

    <!-- add in what we need from symbc -->
    <pathelement path="${jpf-symbc.native_classpath}"/>
    <fileset dir="${jpf-symbc}">
  	  <include name="build/*.jar"/>
    </fileset>

    <!-- our own classes and libs come first -->
    <pathelement location="build/main"/>
    <pathelement location="build/examples"/>
    <fileset dir=".">
  	  <include name="lib/*.jar"/>
    </fileset>

  </path>

  <!-- init: common initialization -->
  <target name="-init">
    <tstamp/>

    <mkdir dir="build"/>               <!-- the build root -->

    <!-- the things that have to be in the classpath of whatever runs Ant -->
    <available property="have_javac" classname="com.sun.tools.javac.Main"/>
    <fail unless="have_javac">no javac found</fail>

    <available file="src/main"        type="dir" property="have_main"/>
    <available file="src/examples"    type="dir" property="have_examples"/>

    <fail unless="have_main">no src/main</fail>
    <fail unless="have_examples">no src/examples</fail>

  </target>

  <!-- ======================= COMPILE SECTION ============================= -->

  <!-- public compile -->
  <target name="compile" depends="-init,-compile-main,-compile-examples"
          description="compile all JPF core sources" >
  </target>

  <target name="-compile-main" if="have_main" >
    <mkdir dir="build/main"/>
    <javac srcdir="src/main" destdir="build/main"
           debug="${debug}" source="${src_level}" deprecation="${deprecation}"
           classpathref="lib.path"/>
  </target>

  <target name="-compile-examples" if="have_examples" depends="-compile-main">
    <mkdir dir="build/examples" />
    <javac srcdir="src/examples" destdir="build/examples"
           debug="${debug}" source="${src_level}" deprecation="${deprecation}">
       <classpath>
         <path refid="lib.path"/>
       </classpath>
    </javac>
  </target>

  <!-- ======================= MISC SECTION ================================ -->

  <!-- build jars -->
  <target name="build" depends="compile,-jar-jvm"
          description="generate the ${ant.project.name} jar files" >
  </target>

  <target name="-jar-jvm">
    <jar jarfile="build/${ant.project.name}.jar">
      <fileset dir="build/main" erroronmissingdir="false"/>
      <fileset dir="build/examples" erroronmissingdir="false"/>
    </jar>
  </target>

  <!-- public clean: cleanup from previous tasks/builds -->
  <target name="clean">
    <delete dir="build" />
    <delete>
      <fileset dir="." includes="**/*~" defaultexcludes="no" />
      <fileset dir="." includes="**/*.bak" defaultexcludes="no" />
      <fileset dir="." includes="**/error.xml" />
    </delete>
  </target>


  <!-- Build Runner Jar File for Badger -->

          <manifest>
              <attribute name="Main-Class" value="edu.cmu.sv.badger.app.BadgerRunner"/>
              <attribute name="Class-Path"

                  string.jar

                  commons-lang3-3.7.jar

          <zipfileset dir="${badger}/build" includes="*.jar" excludes="BadgerRunnerJar.jar"/>
